teaser.text: BP is an energy company: it produces oil and gas, turns some of them into fuels, and delivers energy through contracts, networks and trading. A dollar enters when a customer buys that energy, but what BP keeps depends on the costs and risks of moving it from a field to the customer.

dividend.title: BP dividend
dividend.meta_description: BP dividend payments, cash-flow coverage, plans and yield, explained in plain English.
dividend.opening: BP’s dividend rose from 8.32 to 8.66 cents per quarter. In 2025, dividends and buybacks exceeded BP’s free-cash-flow measure by 11.75 US cents per share, so cash did not cover all shareholder distributions.
dividend.closing: The full memo also answers how BP’s business works, how it compares with rivals, how management allocates capital, and which risks could change the outcome.

blocks.heading: How much does BP pay in dividends?

paragraphs.text: The tables show net debt falling sharply from 2021, then rising between 2024 and 2025. Real free cash flow per share fell from its 2022 peak to 44.64 US cents in 2025; the company’s own free cash flow per share was 51.41 US cents, while dividends and buybacks exceeded it by 11.75 US cents per share. The 5.8% real free-cash-flow yield deducts stock-based pay; enterprise value includes claims ahead of shareholders, while leases sit outside reported net debt. The 4.5% dividend yield is income, not promised total return.

blocks.heading: Is BP’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: In 2022, strong free cash flow supported shareholder payments, debt repayment and acquisitions, including Archaea. As cash generation weakened, BP continued paying dividends and buying back shares. Because those distributions leave the company, BP had to use existing cash, borrow, sell assets or accept less financial flexibility when they exceeded free cash flow.

paragraphs.text: The dividend base case moves from 0.35 dollars per share to 0.379 dollars. The bear case falls to 0.23 dollars, while the bull case reaches 0.423 dollars. The base follows BP’s expectation of at least 4% annual dividend growth and the recent increase from 8.32 to 8.66 cents per quarter. The bear case reflects the risk that weaker cash flow and debt needs override that policy; dividends and buybacks already exceeded BP’s 2025 free-cash-flow measure when combined.

blocks.heading: What is BP’s dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: A dividend is cash paid to shareholders. Its yield measures that payment against the purchase price, but it is not a promised total return because the share price can fall. The dividend increase announced with the second-quarter results therefore helps the income case, but it does not settle the valuation.

earnings.title: BP earnings: guidance and next results
earnings.meta_description: BP expects its next results on October 30, 2026; watch production and refinery throughput against management guidance.
earnings.opening: BP’s next results are expected on October 30, 2026. BP should be watched for production and refinery throughput against the guided ranges.
earnings.closing: The full memo explains how BP makes money, compares BP with rivals, examines BP’s management and sets out BP’s risks.

paragraphs.text: Management guides to 2,180–2,270 thousand boe/d of 2026 production and $13.5–14 billion of capital expenditure. It expects $8–9 billion of 2026 divestment and other proceeds, including about $6 billion from Castrol. By end-2027, it targets net debt of $14–18 billion and structural cost reductions of $5.5–6.5 billion. It targets at least 20% annual compound growth in adjusted free cash flow over 2024–2027 and 16% return on average capital in 2027.

blocks.heading: What should BP watch in the next results?

paragraphs.text: The expected third-quarter results date is October 30, 2026, but that date remains an estimate. Investors should compare production and refinery throughput with management’s guided ranges. Throughput is the amount of crude processed, so it connects refinery availability with potential fuel sales.

Customers is expected to weaken. The important question is whether that decline matches the forecast pressure on Castrol or reflects additional operating problems. Production and refinery reliability will show whether BP can keep equipment working through maintenance and disruption. Strong profit alongside weak physical delivery would make future forecasts more dependent on favourable prices.
